Messages.Body:
On 13 Feb 2002, martijn wrote:

> "Orpheus" <orph...@wanadoo.fr> wrote in message news:<a4e07i$1rk$1...@wanadoo.fr>...

> What would be the point? Temporis is only so so as a discipline.

> I have played a Trujah deck with some weenies with pot and/or pre

> didn't really work either. Not good enough against strong combat
> decks. Not enough stealth to really bleed and the Trujah themselves
> ran out of blood too fast... (temporis really is expensive even more
> so than chimestry).

Put down the crack pipe. The only thing that keeps Temporis balanced is
that there's only three vampires in the whole game who can play it,
they're all huge, and scarce besides.

You are correct that blood management is a major obstacle when building a
Trujah deck. So you build accordingly. The Rack is an obvious choice; it
may seem at first glance that they will lack the interecept to hold onto
it, but you usually end up with more minion actions than you have cards to
get around the NRA rule. So when some stealthy goober comes and takes it,
just tell yourself "one rush action a turn, many combat cards
cycled." After you've erased the poor chump the Rack generally stays on
you, where it belongs. I would suggest The Rack, Brujah/!Brujah HG,
Palatial Estate, *and* Inbase Discoteck (mangled the spelling, I
know). Dumping five pool a turn on Nu, who has tooled up with a couple of
Clotho's, along with whatever Domains you're holding, will do nicely.

I've found Lapse to be one of the most godawfully-good combat cards I've
ever played with, especially mixed in liberally with grapples, signposts,
and potence strikes, as this will allow you to tailor the Lapse to cover
whatever you *don't* happen to be holding in your hand. +2 Strength,
good. How do people adapt to the grapple? By including
maneuvers. Lapse: set range, then grapple... good, and probably more
than anyone can plan for. Uber-Thought's Betrayed... shuts down
everything.... claws, weapons, whatever. Sure, it's expensive, but your
guys are huge, and you have potence, and if you aren't playing Taste of
Vitae with big guys with Potence (and I mean with a big "P"), and who have
known blood management problems besides, then you need your head
examined. So screw the two-blood cost, it's negligible.

Lastly, these are big guys who are in the Freak-Drive club, and who can
govern-down at four blood a turn. What makes the Ventrue so mean? This is
certainly one of their main points of attraction.

My advice is to stay with the deck you described... Nu and Synesios
flanked by four-caps and under split evenly between Brujah and
!Brujah... maybe throw in Sela if you're feeling cocky. Big bleeds with
Legal Manips, some Enchants for lighter bleed and utility, a smattering of
Bum's Rushes, and Free State's Rant. I know how flimsily-anecdotal this
is, but I've won five games in a row with this deck, and the guys I play
with don't suck.

David Cherryholmes
Prince of Durham

actually i found a use for clio's kiss in a small Gio deck :
use the "outferior" version, the one requiring dominate. I discovered it
could be handy a lot of times when i played my Choir deck because it
contains 10 Anarch Troublemaker. Play Anarch troublemaker, next turn tap two
vamps of your prey, play another anarch and bleed at will. Your prey can
still wake and bounce, i guess, but he won't be in the mood for being tapped
again next turn so odds are he'll keep the anarch. On your following turn,
make him lose pool (with no room for redirections) thanks to the Clio's
Kiss. If your opponent doesn't have a hand full of wakes and redirections,
he'll be screwed very soon. Unfortunately you can't use the Clio's Kiss to
retrieve the anarch troublemakers from your ash heap, but it can be handy
for dominate or necro cards...
